newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania blasts Italy for "destabilising" appeal.
newsitem.headline: Albania blasts Italy for "destabilising" appeal.

text.p: Albania issued a strongly worded diplomatic protest to Italy on Tuesday after Rome's deputy foreign minister said the Italian government believed Albanian President Sali Berisha should leave office.

Albania's foreign ministry assailed Italy for meddling in its internal political affairs and Berisha's Democratic party condemned deputy foreign minister Piero Fassino for trying to "destablise" Albania with the remarks.
Fassino said in public in Rome earlier on Tuesday that the embattled Berisha should leave office.
The diplomatic row came as Albania, struggling to restore law and order after weeks of armed anarchy, increased security for judges and worked to repair ransacked jails.

In a further promising sign that the violence and chaos that erupted over failed investment schemes may be abating, several idled factories in the northern district of Shkoder resumed production of clothing and wood processing.
More than 200 people have been killed and 700 injured during the armed rampage in recent weeks that has swept Albania, Europe's poorest nation.
Although Fassino stopped short of calling on Berisha to resign immediately, saying Italy would not push for him to quit now, his remarks were firmly rejected in Tirana.

"We energetically protest against this unacceptable interference in the internal affairs from the Italian Foreign Ministry through the statements of deputy foreign minister Fassino," said the Foreign Ministry statement.
The protest note was handed to the Italian embassy in Tirana. A copy of the letter was distributed via the state-controlled ATA news agency.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whose centre-left government has been badly split over Italy's plans to lead a peacekeeping mission to Albania, quickly distanced himself from Fassino's remarks.
"We are not going to Albania to interfere or get involved in the complex local situation," Prodi told the Italian Senate (upper house) before a scheduled vote on the mission.

"We are going there to offer Albanians the concrete support they need so that they themselves, as is their responsibility, can restore conditions for normal life in their country through free elections."
Relations with Italy were already tense following the sinking last month of a boat filled more than 100 Albanian refugees being pursued by an Italian naval vessel. More than 80 people died.

Italy is expected to lead a U.N.-backed peacekeeping force of some 6,000 soldiers. The troops, who will protect the delivery of emergency food and medicine supplies, are due to start arriving on April 14.
Albania's emergency all-party government, meanwhile, was trying to restore confidence in its judicial system by assigning special police forces to guard judges.
An armoured personel carrier (APC) took up position in front of the Tirana district court, a symbolic gesture as the court -- closed for weeks during the mayhem -- prepared to reopen soon.
"It is up to the court to decide if the suspects are guilty or not," an Interior Ministry official told Reuters. "That is why it is important that the courts reopen as soon as possible."
Although the violence has subsided lately as a night curfew has taken hold, police in the port city of Durres 40 km (25 miles) west of Tirana said three people were killed.

Two mechanics were shot dead after four gunmen drove into a garage, police said. They captured the killers but knew of no motive for the attack. In a separate incident in Durres, a man was shot dead trying to steal a car.

More than 1,300 prisoners held in the nation's seven dilapidated jails escaped or left during the early days of the mayhem that began in early March, with some fleeing convicts destroying and burning wings of the buildings on their way out.

Fewer than 20 prisoners have returned to two jails still operating, but authorities are optimistic many of the 1,309 who left will take advantage of an amnesty programme that cuts jail terms by one-third to those who voluntarily surrender by April 12. About 600 will not have to return because of the amnesty.
